connector: The children have worked out the hardest clue: hundreds of years have passed in Narnia since they left. Today a boat comes round the point with two soldiers and a struggling bundle. Watch how quickly the children act, and listen to what the stranger they rescue tells them about the Narnia of now.

a.raw: lucys knife stayed in its sheath and the children hided among the trees and watched the boat
a.fixed: Lucy’s knife stayed in its sheath, and the children hid among the trees and watched the boat.
a.why: Capital L and an apostrophe in Lucy’s; a comma before and joins two complete thoughts; hid, not hided; a period ends it.

b.raw: peter and susan plunged into the water and they hauled the boat to the bank
b.fixed: Peter and Susan plunged into the water, and they hauled the boat to the bank.
b.why: Capitals on Peter and Susan; a comma before and joins two complete thoughts; a period ends it.

notes.wgrd: Use setting details to learn how this world works: soldiers in steel caps, a Dwarf, stories of ghosts in the woods. Each one is a rule of the new Narnia.
vocab: A place where things meet or connect, especially where train lines split.
A dense group of bushes or small trees growing closely together.
Thorny bushes, especially wild blackberry or raspberry bushes with prickly stems.
Lived in; having people or creatures living there.
notes.wordParts: Prefixes: pre- = before, re- = again or back, trans- = across, inter- = between: preview, return, transport, international.
notes.grammar: Conjunctions join ideas. And adds one idea to another; or offers a choice between them. Stay in the castle or ride into the woods means one, not both. Too many ands in a row give every idea the same weight.
notes.spelling: To split a long word, peel off the prefix and suffix first, then the base is easy: un + familiar, transport + ed, discover + ed.

why.t: In Chapter 2, the children find the treasure chamber of their old castle, dusty and forgotten, its treasures waiting in the dark. Each word you build sets one treasure back in its place. This week’s word parts tell when and where: pre- (before), re- (again), trans- (across) and inter- (between).

wordgame.winDay: Four treasures are back in their niches.
wordgame.win: The treasure chamber is full again, and every torch is lit. pre- = before, re- = again, trans- = across, inter- = between.

virtue.title: Which pillar is it?
virtue.intro: In Chapter 3 the children save a stranger’s life. Read each moment. Tap the pillar it shows best.

items.t: Two soldiers are about to drown a bound Dwarf. Susan shoots; she is very pale, but she is already fitting a second arrow.
items.why: She is scared and acts anyway to save a life.
items.hint: How does Susan feel, and what does she do?

items.t: Peter and Susan plunge into the water fully dressed and haul the boat to the bank.
items.why: They help someone who cannot help himself.

items.t: The Dwarf says, “Ghosts or not, you’ve saved my life and I’m extremely obliged to you.”
items.why: He thanks them properly, even though he doesn’t know who they are.
items.hint: What kind of words does he use?

items.t: The Dwarf says they must hide the boat. Peter says, “I ought to have thought of that myself.”

transcripts.welcome: Hello, it’s Nell. The children have worked out something strange about time in Narnia. Today a boat comes round the point, and they have to decide fast. Today’s question: what does one rescue tell us about the children, and about the Narnia they’ve come back to?
transcripts.read: Read Edmund’s idea about time slowly. It explains everything you’ve seen so far. Then watch the boat. Notice how fast the children act, and listen to the stranger they save. Everything he says is a clue about what Narnia is like now.
transcripts.spelling: Long words look scary until you take them apart. Peel off the beginning and the ending first. What’s left is usually a word you already know. Unhappy: take off un, and there’s happy. Then the syllables almost split themselves.
